title: Surbhi Rathore - Agentic AI Is a UX Problem Disguised as a Technology Breakthrough

segments.text: SURBHI RATHORE: Hey, everyone.
Hope you're having a good time.
We have spent the last day and majority of the day
today talking about how are we building agents in the best way,
monitoring them, orchestrating them, evolving them.
But I'm going to spend the next five minutes giving you
a little different perspective on the reason
why we're building all these agents,
is that consumers trust them to use and operate.
And a lot of this is a UX problem and not
a technology and model problem.
I am the VP of AI products in a company called Invoca.
We build marketing and revenue agents
for brands which operate in highly considered purchases.
Before I joined Invoca last year,
I was the former CEO co-founder of a company called
symbl.ai for seven years.
Our company was acquired last year.
And we spent seven years on the infrastructure bit.
We, ourselves, spent a lot of money and time training language
models which were very specific to understand the nuances
of human-to-human interactions.
And of course, my hypothesis has massively
evolved over the last one and a half years--
or one year since deploying these agents.
And using the models have somewhat become interchangeable.
But really, what matters is, how the design of these models
and the experience with the consumer will dictate
whether whatever you build the agent that
was capable of performing the workflow actually influenced
in the right moment with the right timing.
So just to give a little background
and the type of persona I'm talking about today,
Invoca operates in an industry called considered purchases,
where we work with companies with health care, telco,
insurance, home services, where the consumer, almost every time,
needs to speak to a human before making a purchase decision.
These are not things that you operate on a day-to-day basis.
And in these industries, earning trust
almost needs to be instant.
And agents that operate in these industries
have to emulate the human trust that the consumers have
been working for years with these brands
almost immediately through the way that they're
interacting with the consumer.
The big problem here is not really
to define workflows and do revenue operations
or do agentic commerce.
The bigger workflow is to actually win
the user trust that is arriving when they're
interacting with the agents with their already failed mindset.
Your users and the consumers that we work with day in and day
out are so skeptical of interacting with agents.
And that's not because of their paranoia about AI.
It's really because of years of gaps in technology
that we have all been through and failed
UX of the agent experiences or conversational AI
experiences that have been operating for a long time.
So when your user starts operating with these systems,
they're thinking that, oh, I'll have
to repeat all the information.
This agent doesn't know anything about me.
And I'm just going to say, talk to a human,
and just get rid of this loop very fast.
So that's why the hardest design problem
is in making the agent capable.
It's actually making it trustworthy to someone
that's walked in expecting it to fail.
So to solve these problems, we have
started to build a context layer that
specifically informs the UX.
Invoca has operated over the last, I think, 14 years,
and they contain huge volumes of call information, buyer journey
data, interaction data.
And all that, we are mining to inform
the knowledge and the training of the agents,
to inform what intents they operate, what actions they take.
And that's all great, but we're building
another layer that just informs the UX of the agent itself.
And it sort of falls into three categories.
One is, of course, what do you know
about the consumer before the consumer even types the word?,
which is the context-fed UX.
The second is the graduated agency,
where, at the time where you're designing the agent,
you're really giving the agent the things that it should do
and it should not do, and designing the experience for it.
And the third is the in-moment reading,
which is actually one of the most important things,
because if you feel that there is
urgency or something off the happy path
that a consumer is facing with, how
do you skip the usual normal path
and design a workflow that gets the consumer
a delightful experience in that moment?
So these are just examples, and I'm
going to go through quickly because of time here.
But this is an oncology example, a patient trying to book
an appointment, 2:15, after detecting cancer,
and not available in the form fill.
And instead of taking them through a painful experience
of filling a form, the agent quickly books an appointment
and confirms availability of doctors for that.
The second one is around prescription refills
where the hospital has implemented a new MyChart
system.
They want the self-serve, the experience.
But again, the timing after 6:00 PM,
trying to get a refill in place, left a voicemail, no response,
and the agent quickly diverts them to the right experience
to handle it quickly.
The third one is just an example of how the same UX can
be applied to support use cases, although we've
spent a majority of time on revenue-generating use cases,
where someone is operating in the morning-- waiting
for a video interview call in the morning,
and internet is down.
So how do you handle diagnosis not through a 20-step process,
but a five-step self-diagnosis, and stay with the call?
So yeah, because we're running short on time,
but just leaving you with this thought
that, as you're all designing experiences for your agent,
think about the user experience and really think about context
being a key input to the design system for your agents,
and if you don't have the data collected
and build an agentic loop, or connect to systems that actually
power that data.
Thank you so much.
